name: Question 9
problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda =3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Question 9
?

A=[−8−4−8−92−2915]

The matrix above has eigenvalues λ1=λ2=−2 and λ3=3. Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.

a
[3100−2100−2]
b
[3000−2100−2]
c
[31003000−2]
d
[30003000−2]
e
[3000−2000−2]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that we are given a 3×3 matrix with the following eigenvalues:

  • λ=−2 of algebraic multiplicity 2

  • λ=3 of algebraic multiplicity 1

As a result, we have one 1×1 Jordan block J1(3) corresponding to λ=3. However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to λ=−2:

  • Case I. We may get the single 2×2 Jordan block J2(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chain: v2→A+2Iv1→A+2I0
  • Case II. We may get a composition of two 1×1 Jordan blocks, namely J1(−2)⊕J1(−2). This happens when the generalized eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chains: v1→A+2I0v2→A+2I0

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to λ=−2.

Computing A+2I, we get

A+2I=[−8−4−8−92−2915]+2[100010001]=[−6−4−8−94−2917].

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

A+2I=[−6−4−8−94−2917]R2:=R2+(−32)R1R3:=R3+32R1∼[−6−4−8010100−5−5]R3:=R3+12R2∼[−6−4−801010000]

Since nullity(A+2I)=1, there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−2, say, v1. So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−2 form the following chain:

v2→A+2Iv1→A+2I0

Therefore, we have case I, and A has the following Jordan canonical form:

J1(3)⊕J2(−2)=[3000−2100−2]

Note: The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
